result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.ada_star_search()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find path using ADA* (Anytime Dynamic A*) search algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L29438-L29668){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.ada_star_search( source, target, epsilon=1.0, weight_attr="weight", heuristic=None, reuse_planner=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![ADA* search](/assets/graphs/ada-star-search.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A directed weighted graph with three routes from A to F, costing 4, 6, and 5. With epsilon 1.0 ADA* behaves like A* and returns the optimal path A, B, C, F, drawn in the accent color. The card gives its cost, 1 + 2 + 1 = 4." width="100%"} ADA* is an anytime optimal pathfinding algorithm that can return suboptimal paths quickly and iteratively improve them. The epsilon parameter controls the trade-off between solution quality and speed. The search finds the path from `source=` to `target=` with the lowest total edge weight. It is guided by an optional heuristic, an estimate of the remaining distance, which lets it skip parts of the graph that are clearly off course. Multiplying the heuristic by `epsilon=` makes the search greedier: it settles on a path sooner, and that path is guaranteed to cost at most `epsilon` times the optimum. Lowering `epsilon=` on later calls (with `reuse_planner=True`) refines the same search rather than starting over. This is useful for: - route planning on spatial graphs (road networks, grids, game maps) where a geometric distance makes a good heuristic - time-constrained settings where a good-enough path now is better than the best path later - interactive tools that show a quick answer first and then improve it Some details to be aware of: - edge weights come from each edge's `weight` value (as set with `add_edge(weight=...)`), falling back to the edge attribute named by `weight_attr=`, and finally to `1.0`. The graph does not need to be created with `weighted=True` - in directed graphs the path follows edge directions; undirected edges can be used both ways. Weights should be non-negative - without a heuristic the search is equivalent to Dijkstra's algorithm and `epsilon=` has no effect - the search runs *backward* from `target=`, so the heuristic is called as `heuristic(node_id, source_id)` and must estimate the distance between a node and the *source* - each expansion scans the edge list, so the method is best suited to small and medium-sized graphs; for plain shortest paths on large graphs use `shortest_path()` ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Starting node, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An unknown label raises a `ValueError`. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Destination node, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An unknown label raises a `ValueError`. [epsilon]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Suboptimality bound; should be at least `1.0`. Defaults to `1.0`, which finds an optimal path (as plain A*). With `epsilon > 1.0`, the heuristic is inflated by this factor: the search explores fewer nodes and the returned path costs at most `epsilon` times the optimum. Has no effect when `heuristic=` is `None`. [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["weight"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to read weights from, for edges that have no `weight` value of their own. Defaults to `"weight"`. Edges with neither a `weight` value nor this attribute (or with a non-numeric one) cost `1.0`. [heuristic]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[Callable[[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]], float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Function `h(node_id, source_id) -> float` estimating the path cost between a node and the source node. Both arguments are always integer node IDs (use `get_label_from_id()` or `get_node()` inside the function to look up labels or attributes). For an optimal result with `epsilon=1.0` it must be admissible, never overestimating the true cost. If the function raises an exception or returns a non-numeric value, `0.0` is used silently. If `None` (default), a zero heuristic is used, which is equivalent to Dijkstra's algorithm. [reuse_planner]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, keep the planner (stored on the graph) so that a later call with the same `source=`, `target=`, and `weight_attr=` continues the existing search instead of starting a new one. This is how you refine a quick result: call first with a large `epsilon=`, then again with smaller values. The match is on the values exactly as passed (a label and the equivalent ID count as different), the `heuristic=` of the original call is kept, and only one planner is stored at a time. If `False` (default), every call builds a fresh planner. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Path from source to target as list of node IDs, starting with the source and ending with the target. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or target nodes don't exist, or if no path exists. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Anytime Dynamic A* (Likhachev et al., 2005) sits between A* and D* Lite: it can return a first, provably $\epsilon$-suboptimal path very quickly, then refine that same search when $\epsilon$ is lowered on a subsequent call. Setting `epsilon=1.0` recovers ordinary A* optimality; larger $\epsilon$ inflates the heuristic so the search prunes more aggressively, trading path length for speed. The underlying search runs backward from `target=` to `source=`, which is what lets it reuse work when the goal is fixed but the source or graph weights change. Passing `reuse_planner=True` keeps the planner alive between calls (stashed on `graph._ada_star_planner`) and is the usual pattern for iterative deepening: warm-start at a large $\epsilon$, then feed a shrinking sequence. A call with a different source or target pair replaces the stored planner with a new one. ## Examples {.doc-examples} From A to D there are three routes: A-B-D (cost `1 + 5 = 6`), A-C-D (cost `4 + 1 = 5`), and A-B-C-D (cost `1 + 2 + 1 = 4`). Weights are set with `weight=` and, without a heuristic, the search finds the cheapest route, which is also the longest in hops: ::: {#b88ada88 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes( [ ("A", {"x": 0.0, "y": 0.0}), ("B", {"x": 1.0, "y": 0.0}), ("C", {"x": 1.0, "y": 2.0}), ("D", {"x": 2.0, "y": 2.0}), ] ) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 1.0), ("A", "C", 4.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "D", 1.0), ("B", "D", 5.0), ] ) ) path = graph.ada_star_search("A", "D") [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in path] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'] ``` ::: ::: The nodes above carry `x` and `y` coordinates, and the straight-line distance between two nodes never exceeds the cost of the route between them, so it is an admissible heuristic. The function receives node IDs and looks up the coordinates with `get_node()`. With `epsilon=1.0` the result is still optimal; with `epsilon=5.0` the inflated heuristic makes the search settle early on the more expensive A-B-D route (cost `6`, within the bound of `5 * 4`): ::: {#5126a0aa .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} def euclidean(node_id, source_id): a = graph.get_node(node_id).attributes b = graph.get_node(source_id).attributes return ((a["x"] - b["x"]) ** 2 + (a["y"] - b["y"]) ** 2) ** 0.5 optimal = graph.ada_star_search("A", "D", heuristic=euclidean, epsilon=1.0) greedy = graph.ada_star_search("A", "D", heuristic=euclidean, epsilon=5.0) ( [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in optimal], [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in greedy], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'], ['A', 'B', 'D']) ``` ::: ::: With `reuse_planner=True`, a quick, greedy first answer can be refined by calling again with a smaller `epsilon=`. The second call continues the stored search and reaches the optimal route: ::: {#06652c8c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} first = graph.ada_star_search( "A", "D", heuristic=euclidean, epsilon=5.0, reuse_planner=True ) refined = graph.ada_star_search("A", "D", epsilon=1.0, reuse_planner=True) ( [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in first], [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in refined], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (['A', 'B', 'D'], ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']) ``` ::: ::: Weights can also come from any other numeric edge attribute through `weight_attr=`. Here the costs are stored under `cost`; without `weight_attr="cost"` every edge would cost `1.0` and the two-hop route A-B-D would win: ::: {#0b966d15 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} costs = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", {"cost": 1.0}), ("A", "C", {"cost": 4.0}), ("B", "C", {"cost": 2.0}), ("C", "D", {"cost": 1.0}), ("B", "D", {"cost": 5.0}), ] ) ) ( [costs.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in costs.ada_star_search("A", "D")], [ costs.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in costs.ada_star_search("A", "D", weight_attr="cost") ], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (['A', 'B', 'D'], ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']) ``` ::: :::
